notes.meaning: God poured out His full fury against Egypt through heavenly messengers who brought disaster. These angels were not evil in their own nature, but they were called destroying angels because they carried out God's severe punishment. This fierce display of divine anger was the final and most terrible plague.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars understand the band of angels not as spiritual beings, but as a poetic way of describing the fierce anger, fury, and calamity sent upon Egypt.

notes.meaning: The Lord cleared a direct path for His righteous anger, removing every obstacle in the way of His justice. He showed no mercy to those who hardened their hearts against Him, handing them over to deadly disease. His judgment struck Egypt completely and without delay.

God struck down every firstborn son across the entire land of Egypt. The Bible calls them the firstfruits of strength in the tents of Ham, because the Egyptians were descended from Noah's son Ham. This sudden blow broke Pharaoh's stubborn pride and forced him to let God's people go.

The Lord brought Israel out of Egypt and led them like a shepherd guiding a flock of sheep. Even though the people were weak, timid, and defenseless, God watched over them with tender care in the barren desert. His gentle leadership showed that He was their true protector.

God kept His people safe so they did not need to fear, even when danger seemed near. When the Egyptian army chased after them into the sea, the waters returned and drowned every pursuer. God faithfully protects those who belong to Him while destroying their enemies.

The Lord brought His people safely to the borders of the Promised Land, a hilly country He had set apart for Himself. God acquired this mountain region by His own mighty power and right hand. Every blessing His people enjoy is won by His strength alone.

God drove out the pagan nations that lived in Canaan and divided the land among the tribes of Israel. Each tribe received its measured share by lot, just as the Lord had promised. The Israelites were then able to settle down in homes and cities they had not built.

Even after settling in their new home, the Israelites rebelled against God Most High during the time of the judges. They tested His patience by ignoring His laws and refusing to keep His commands. Receiving great blessings does not keep a sinful heart from going astray.

The new generation turned away from God, proving just as unfaithful as their parents before them. They were like a faulty or crooked bow that snaps or shoots wide of the mark, failing the archer when needed most. Their promises of loyalty could not be trusted.

The people made God angry by building hilltop shrines and bowing down to carved statues. This idolatry, which means worshiping created things instead of the living God, was like unfaithfulness in marriage and provoked His holy jealousy. God will never share His rightful praise with false gods.

God heard their false prayers and saw their idol worship, and His holy anger burned against Israel. He rejected the nation for a time because of their constant rebellion. God sees every secret act of unfaithfulness and will not let sin go unanswered.

The Lord walked away from the tabernacle at Shiloh, which was the holy tent where He had chosen to live among human beings. He abandoned this site because the priests were wicked and the people served idols. God's special presence departed from Shiloh, and the ark never returned there again.

God allowed His ark, the sacred chest that represented His power and splendor, to be captured by the enemy Philistines. Even though the ark was Israel's most precious sign of God's presence, the Lord gave it up to humble His rebellious people. Holy symbols cannot protect those who abandon the Lord.

Because God was enraged by the sins of His people, He surrendered them to the Philistine sword. Thousands of soldiers fell on the battlefield in a single day. When people forsake God, they lose the protection of His hand.

The fire of war and slaughter consumed the best young men of Israel. Because so many young men died on the battlefield, the young women had no one to marry, leaving the land without joyful wedding songs. Sin brought terrible grief and emptied the towns of celebration.

The priests, including Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas, were killed by the Philistine sword. The calamity was so sudden and overwhelming that their widows could not even hold proper funeral services to weep for them. God's holy justice reaches even those who hold sacred offices when they practice evil.

After seeming to hold back while His people suffered, the Lord suddenly stepped forward to act. He is described like a mighty warrior refreshed and emboldened by wine, shouting loudly as he charges into battle. God may seem silent for a season, but He never forgets to defend His name.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern commentators and translations view this image as describing a warrior shouting in a drunken fury rather than a champion refreshed by a moderate drink.

notes.meaning: The Lord struck His Philistine enemies with painful plagues and forced them to retreat in shame. He brought lasting disgrace upon them, forcing them to return the captured ark with models of their plagues as a sign of their defeat. God always triumphs over those who mock His power.

God chose not to return His sacred dwelling place to the territory of Ephraim, the son of Joseph. The sanctuary at Shiloh had lost its privilege because of the people's long history of sin. God removed leadership from a tribe that had failed to honor Him.

Instead of Ephraim, the Lord chose the southern tribe of Judah and Mount Zion in Jerusalem, which He loved. He made this hill the new home for His presence and the center of true worship. God's choices are based on His gracious love and His faithful promises.

The Lord had Solomon build a magnificent temple on Mount Zion that stood firm and high like the hills. Unlike the portable tent that moved through the wilderness, this stone sanctuary was built to last as securely as the earth itself. It stood as a visible sign of God's enduring majesty.

God selected David to be His servant and the ruler over Israel, choosing him from the sheep pastures. David was the youngest in his family, but God took him from simple, hard work to sit upon the royal throne. God delights in lifting up humble, faithful workers to carry out His great plans.

David had spent his youth gently caring for mother sheep and their newborn lambs. The Lord used that practical experience to prepare David to care for the nation of Israel as his flock. David's shepherd heart pointed ahead to Jesus, the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for His sheep.

David led the people of Israel with an honest heart, seeking God's glory and the good of the nation instead of selfish power. He also guided them with skillful hands, using wisdom and military ability to protect the realm. True leadership requires both moral honesty and practical skill.
